questions.text: A 1000 mm escalator operates at Salvan's rated-speed limit of 38 m/min (the maximum allowed along the incline) and is projected to carry 5,500 passengers/hour during peak periods. If demand increases and a second identical escalator is installed, what is the total system capacity, and what factors could limit this theoretical maximum?

options.text: 11,000 persons/hour with no limiting factors, assuming perfect conditions
11,000 persons/hour maximum theoretical; actual throughput limited by landing congestion, dwell time, and step spacing geometry
7,500 persons/hour; the second escalator reduces individual capacity by interference effects
6,750 persons/hour per unit; two units operate at reduced speed to prevent overloading

questions.rationale: Two identical escalators can theoretically deliver 11,000 persons/hour (2 x 5,500). Actual throughput is limited by landing congestion, passenger dwell time on steps, step spacing geometry, and balancing passenger loads between units. The speed basis is aligned to Salvan's rated-speed limit of 38 m/min used in the article body. Source: Salvan Architectural Utilities 2 (escalator rated speed max 38 m/min along the incline).

questions.text: What control requirement applies to escalator starting switches?

options.text: They must be hidden from every landing.
They may be ordinary wall switches in a storage room.
They are unnecessary if an emergency brake exists.
They must be key-operated and located within sight of the steps.

questions.rationale: They must be key-operated and located within sight of the steps. This answer matches Salvan Utilities 2 refined markdown lines 1727-1736.

questions.text: What is the maximum rated speed allowed for an escalator per the checked PH regulatory extract (Salvan), measured along the incline?

options.text: 0.35 m/s (about 21 m/min)
0.5 m/s (about 30 m/min)
38 m/min (about 0.63 m/s)
1.0 m/s (about 60 m/min)

questions.rationale: Salvan's regulatory extract (used as the speed basis throughout the article body) states that an escalator's rated speed, measured along the incline, must not be more than 38 m per minute (~0.63 m/s). The original '0.5 m/s' (~30 m/min) answer is not the value used in the article body and has been replaced to keep a single consistent speed basis. Source: Salvan Architectural Utilities 2 (escalator rated speed max 38 m/min along the incline).

questions.text: An escalator operates at Salvan's maximum rated speed of 38 m/min (~0.63 m/s) along the incline, with 1000 mm width. How does operating at this rated-speed limit affect the design requirements compared with a slower installation?

options.text: No design changes; speed affects only throughput, not safety systems

Enhanced safety systems are required including stronger handrail drive and guardrail reinforcement, because faster passenger movement increases forces on handrails, balustrades, and emergency stopping mechanisms
Wider step spacing is required to accommodate the higher velocity
The balustrade height must be increased by 200 mm minimum

questions.rationale: Installations at the rated-speed limit (38 m/min, ~0.63 m/s, per Salvan's PH regulatory extract used in the article body) require enhanced safety systems because faster passenger movement increases forces on handrails, balustrades, and emergency stopping mechanisms. The original 0.65 m/s framing has been replaced with the article body's 38 m/min basis for a single consistent speed basis. Source: Salvan Architectural Utilities 2 (escalator rated speed max 38 m/min along the incline).

questions.text: What is the source-safe fire-protection concern for escalators piercing several floors?

options.text: Escalators do not affect fire spread.
The floor opening can spread smoke or fire and needs an approved protection method.
Only the tread finish controls fire safety.
Fire protection is optional if the escalator is reversible.

questions.rationale: The floor opening can spread smoke or fire and needs an approved protection method. This answer matches Salvan Utilities 2 refined markdown lines 16445-16501.

questions.text: A building owner compares two escalator specifications for a new shopping center: Option A (800 mm step width, 30 m/min, 30 deg inclination) vs. Option B (1000 mm step width, 38 m/min rated-speed limit, 35 deg maximum inclination). What are the implications of choosing Option B?

options.text: Option B provides higher capacity with minimal additional cost; always preferred for commercial projects

Option B provides higher theoretical capacity but requires enhanced safety systems, higher motor power (kW), stronger structural support, and increased maintenance complexity because it operates at the rated-speed (38 m/min) and inclination (35 deg) limits
Option B reduces energy consumption by using maximum inclination; it is more efficient than Option A
Option B is identical in safety profile to Option A; the choice depends only on aesthetic preferences

questions.rationale: Option B (1000 mm, 38 m/min rated-speed limit, 35 deg maximum inclination) leverages maximum design parameters across width, speed, and inclination. This delivers higher capacity but demands enhanced safety systems (reinforced balustrades, stronger emergency stops), larger motors, heavier structural loads, and more intensive maintenance because it operates at the rated-speed and inclination limits. The original 0.5 m/s / 0.65 m/s speed bases have been replaced with the article body's 38 m/min basis for a single consistent speed basis. Source: Salvan Architectural Utilities 2 (escalator rated speed max 38 m/min along the incline; inclination max 35 deg).
